title.text: Did Franklin (from problem D) succeed in massacring a village of innocent elves like Frieren and Dilhan (from problem E)?

children.text: The official lore is that he got lost in a forest of oddly colored Christmas trees (from problem F) and decided instead to write this editorial.
What can we say about the number of 'Yes's.
Consider the number of 'Yes's in the string, and what happens to this number during an operation.
In any operation, there are two things we are allowed to do:
Convert a 'Yes' and a 'No' into a 'Yes'
In either operation the number of 'Yes's remains unchanged.
This means that if we start with at least two 'Yes's, then the final state must contain at least two 'Yes's, and cannot be a single character.

On the other hand, if we start with at most one 'Yes', then any operation we do will be legal, as there will not be two 'Yes's to combine. This means we can do any $$$n - 1$$$ operations, and we will be left with a single character.
Thus, the answer to the question is 'Yes' if and only if the input string contains at most one 'Y'.
You have a suspicious string. For a fixed u, suppose the closest s is two characters to the right. Where must the other s be?
It must be two characters to the left. In particular, the two s's must be on opposite sides of the u.

You have a suspicious string. Suppose there are two consecutive u's. Let the closest s to the left u is three characters to the left. Where must the other s be? Where must the closest s's to the right u be?

The s must be three characters to the right, which is two characters to the right of the right u. However, this implies that there must be a corresponding s two characters to the left, which would be the closest s of the left u. By this reasoning, there cannot be two consecutive u's.

Consider a single $$$\mathtt{u}$$$ at index $$$i$$$ in a suspicious string $$$w$$$. The two closest $$$\mathtt{s}$$$ have some distance $$$d$$$ from the $$$\mathtt{u}$$$, and only $$$w_{u-d}$$$ and $$$w_{u+d}$$$ have distance $$$d$$$ from $$$w_i$$$. Therefore, the two closest $$$\mathtt{s}$$$ must be on opposite sides of the $$$\mathtt{u}$$$. This means that no $$$\mathtt{u}$$$ can be on either end of a suspicious string, so a given $$$w_i = \mathtt{u}$$$ must have two neighbors:

If it has a $$$\mathtt{u}$$$ on one side and a $$$\mathtt{s}$$$ on another side, the string is not suspicious — the closest $$$\mathtt{s}$$$ has distance $$$1$$$, but the next closest $$$\mathtt{s}$$$ has distance greater than $$$1$$$.

If it has a $$$\mathtt{u}$$$ on each side, it is in the middle of a larger run of $$$\mathtt{u}$$$'s. This run must eventually end with a $$$\mathtt{u}$$$ that is either on an end of the string, or has a $$$\mathtt{u}$$$ and $$$\mathtt{s}$$$ as its two neighbors. Both are illegal.
If it has a $$$\mathtt{s}$$$ on each side, there is no issue – the two closest $$$\mathtt{s}$$$ have distance $$$1$$$ from the $$$\mathtt{u}$$$.
Therefore, a string is suspicious if and only if:
The first and last characters are $$$\mathtt{s}$$$, and
The neighbors of each $$$\mathtt{u}$$$ are $$$\mathtt{s}$$$ — i.e., no two $$$\mathtt{u}$$$'s are adjacent.
To make a string $$$r$$$ suspicious, we can then do the following:
If $$$r_1 = \mathtt{u}$$$, set it to $$$\mathtt{s}$$$. Repeat for $$$r_n$$$ (where $$$n$$$ is the length of $$$r$$$).
Iterate left to right through the string (increasing order in the index $$$i$$$); if, taking past operations into account, $$$r_i = r_{i-1} = \mathtt{u}$$$, then set $$$r_i = \mathtt{s}$$$.
This greedy algorithm makes the string suspicious; it remains to show that this minimizes the number of operations.

The first step is clearly required and thus optimal. To see that the second step is optimal, consider taking a run of $$$\mathtt{u}$$$'s and pairing up adjacent $$$\mathtt{u}$$$'s from left to right — e.g., $$$\mathtt{s} \ \color{red}{\underline{\mathtt{uu}} \ \underline{\mathtt{uu}} \ \mathtt{u}} \ \mathtt{s}$$$. In each pair, at least one $$$\mathtt{u}$$$ must be changed to an $$$\mathtt{s}$$$ in order to satisfy the condition that no two $$$\mathtt{u}$$$'s are adjacent. The above algorithm changes exactly the second $$$\mathtt{u}$$$ in each pair, so it achieves this lower bound. (Specifically, for each run of length $$$k$$$, it performs $$$\lfloor k/2 \rfloor$$$ operations.)
Running the algorithm and counting the number of operations it performs solves this problem in $$$O(n)$$$.

Optionally, to make the below implementations cleaner, we prepend and append a $$$\mathtt{u}$$$ to the string, then skip the first step of the above algorithm and perform the second step only. This results in the same number of operations. (Why?)

The number of children on the naughty and nice lists combined will be $$$n-1$$$. However, not all assignments to the naughty and nice lists are possible. Try figuring out exactly which assignments are possible.
Exactly one child will not be chosen by Santa. If we fix/decide which child this will be, what can we say about the other children?

Note that $$$n - 1$$$ of the children will be chosen by Santa, and one will remain unchosen. We can compute the best possible answer for each option of unchosen child and compute the answer at the end.
First, note that the first child in line will always have a contribution of $$$+a_i$$$ (unless they are the unchosen child).

For any child to the right of the unchosen child, the only way they can be chosen is to be put on the naughty list (as the unchosen child will always be ahead of them in line). This means that all of their contribution to $$$X$$$ must be $$$-a_i$$$.

For any child in between the first child and the unchosen child, if their niceness is $$$a_i$$$, the contribution added by assigning them to the nice or naughty list will always be $$$+a_i$$$ or $$$-a_i$$$. It turns out that for each of the children in this range, we can choose each of their signs independently (and no matter what we choose, it is a valid assignment). We shall show this by construction. After determining what sign we want each child to be, we perform the following strategy: If we want the second child to be negative, perform an operation of type 2 (putting the second child on the naughty list). Otherwise, perform an operation of type 1 and put the first child on the nice list. Whenever we do the second case the new child in the first position will either be one from whom we want a positive contribution, or the fixed unchosen child.
As we wish to maximize the total score, for each child between the first and unchosen child we will make their value equal to $$$\max(+a_i, -a_i) = |a_i|$$$.

Now if we naively compute the optimal value for each choice of unchosen child, this will take $$$\mathcal{O}(n^2)$$$ time. To optimize this we can employ prefix/suffix sums. If we pre-compute the prefix sums of $$$|a_i|$$$ (except $$$a_1$$$ which does not have an absolute value), and compute the suffix sums of $$$-a_i$$$ then for any fixed unchosen child we can compute the maximum value of $$$X$$$ by adding the prefix sum of $$$|a_i|$$$ before the unchosen child and the suffix sum of $$$-a_i$$$ after the unchosen child (adding in $$$a_1$$$ if the unchosen child is not the first child).
After computing these $$$n$$$ values, we can take the maximum to find the overall maximum value of $$$X$$$.
Fix the $$$m$$$ surviving elves. They must have attacked. Who are the targets of these attacks? What happens to those targets?
Each surviving elf must have attacked a smaller elf. Those elves die.
Find an upper bound on the number of elves that can survive.

For each surviving elf, there must be a corresponding target elf that it attacks, which dies immediately (and cannot be attacked by other surviving elves). Therefore, at most $$$\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$$$ elves can survive.
Once the elves that survive are fixed, and the elves they attack are fixed, there may be some remaining elves, which should not survive. Find a way to deal with them.
$$$m=0$$$ must be handled separately (why?). The hardest part is killing the strongest elf. Figure out when it is possible and how to do so.
Note that in each attack, at least one elf dies. The elf with smaller attack value must die, as its health is always at most its attack, which in turn is less than the other elf's attack.

Consider the elves that survive at the end. They each must attack once, and since they survived, each elf they attacked must have died. Furthermore, each target elf can only be attacked by one surviving elf, as they will die immediately upon being attacked. Therefore, for every surviving elf, there must be a corresponding dead elf. This means that no more than $$$\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$$$ elves can survive, so if $$$2m \gt n$$$, output $$$-1$$$.
Now, suppose $$$2m \le n$$$. $$$m$$$ elves survive and they attack $$$m$$$ smaller target elves, which die. We need the $$$n - 2m$$$ leftover elves to die. How can we do this?

We can sort the leftover elves from left to right. Then, each leftover elf attacks the larger elf immediately after it from left to right. This causes all leftover elves to die except for the largest. If there is a target elf which dies ($$$m \gt 0$$$), we can also kill the largest elf — let it attack a larger target elf before that target elf is attacked by some larger surviving elf. This will kill the largest leftover elf, while allowing the target elf it attacks to still be alive for the larger surviving elf.

This idea solves the problem for $$$0 \lt m \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$$$ — a construction always exists in this case. One clean way to implement this is by sorting all elves by their size, letting the largest $$$m$$$ elves be the surviving elves, the next largest $$$m$$$ elves be the target elves, and the remaining (smallest) $$$n-2m$$$ elves be the leftover elves. Each leftover elf attacks the elf to its right, and then each surviving elf attacks a different target elf. In the end, every surviving elf has attacked.

For $$$m = 0$$$, the idea to kill the leftover elves is not sufficient because the largest leftover elf has no one larger to attack and thus will not die. To kill the largest elf, we need some elves to attack it; all of them will die. We can then deal with the remaining elves using the same idea for the leftover elves above.

To implement the $$$m = 0$$$ case, sort the elves. Iterate through the elves in decreasing order from the second-largest elf until their sum reaches the largest elf's health; save these elves to attack the largest elf at the end. Each remaining smaller elf should attack the (larger) elf to its right and die in the process; then let the saved elves should attack the largest elf so that all elves die.

If all other elves attacking the largest elf is not sufficient to kill the largest elf (i.e., the sum of all elves except the largest is less than the largest elf), there is no way to kill the largest elf. In this case it is not possible for $$$0$$$ elves to survive, so output $$$-1$$$.
This solves the problem in all cases in $$$\mathcal{O}(n \log n)$$$.
What are the properties/invariants of the flatten operation? Use this to find an invariant on $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$.
The sum of the entire array is invariant under the flatten operation. This means $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$ always have the same sum.
Assume there are no flatten operations after the final concatenate (why?). Can we find where in the hidden array $$$a$$$ the final concatenate happened?
From the previous hint, the final array can be split into the two arrays before the final concatenate. Which array contains the maximum?

The two arrays were flattened from some common ancestor — i.e., they were once equal before being flattened into their state just before the final concatenate. Only flatten operations have happened since they were equal.
If one array was flattened more times than the other, which contains the maximum?
How can you tell which array was flattened more times?

Flattening is an operation that intuitively "pushes down" the maximum; the array that is flattened fewer times is guaranteed to contain the maximum. Flattening also increases the length of the array by $$$1$$$, so the shorter array contains the maximum.
Define $$$ab$$$ to be the concatenation of $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$.

Observe that flattening an array preserves its sum. In addition, $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$ initially have the same sum, and they have the same sum after concatenation. Therefore, $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$ always have the same sum when applying the given operations.

All flatten operations after the final concatenate can be considered to be before the concatenate, as any flatten operations on $$$ab$$$ are also legal flatten operations on either $$$a$$$ or $$$b$$$ (the maximum of $$$ab$$$ is a maximum of either $$$a$$$ or $$$b$$$). Thus, assume the final operation is a concatenate.

Consider the arrays $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$ before the final concatenate, so that the hidden final array is $$$ab$$$. Since $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$ have the same sum, we can find where the split point in $$$ab$$$ is using binary search on prefix sums. The maximum of $$$ab$$$ must be in either $$$a$$$ or $$$b$$$. How can we determine which one it is in?
Claim: The shorter of $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$ must contain a maximum of $$$ab$$$.

Some number of flatten operations before the final concatenate, $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$ were identical — either after the previous concatenate, or at the beginning of the process (when $$$a = b = [2^k]$$$) if no prior concatenate existed. Since flattening increases the size of an array by $$$1$$$, the shorter of $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$ was flattened fewer times. Intuitively, flattening reduces the maximum over time, so the array that is flattened fewer times contains the maximum. More formally, suppose one array is flattened $$$x$$$ times and the other is flattened $$$y$$$ times, with $$$x \ge y$$$. After each array is flattened $$$y$$$ times, both arrays contain the same multiset of elements. Flattening the array the remaining $$$x - y$$$ times cannot increase its maximum, so the maximum of the array that is flattened more times cannot exceed the maximum of the other array. Therefore, the shorter of $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$, which is flattened fewer (or equal) times, contains a maximum of $$$ab$$$.

Now, for a final array $$$ab$$$, we know which of $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$ is guaranteed to contain a maximum of $$$ab$$$. Note that $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$ are both arrays that can be generated by the given operations. This means we can recurse on whichever contains the maximum.
This leads to the following algorithm:
Using binary search on prefix sums, find the split point of the final $$$ab$$$ — i.e., find $$$m$$$ such that $$$2(a_1 + \cdots + a_m) = a_1 + \cdots + a_n$$$.
Recurse on the shorter of $$$[a_1, \ldots, a_m]$$$ and $$$[a_{m+1}, \ldots, a_n]$$$.

In the base case of this recursive algorithm, we have an array $$$a$$$ which was never concatenated. If $$$a$$$ was never flattened, then its length is $$$1$$$, and we can simply query and return its only element. Otherwise, the array $$$a = [2^k]$$$ was flattened at some point into $$$[2^{k-1}, 2^{k-1}]$$$ and has length at least $$$2$$$. But $$$[2^{k-1}, 2^{k-1}]$$$ can be generated by starting with $$$[2^{k-1}]$$$ and concatenating, so if $$$a$$$ has length at least $$$2$$$, we can assume there were more concatenates and continue recursing. Thus, the only base case we need is $$$n = 1$$$.

Since the size of the array decreases by at least a factor of $$$2$$$ in each recursive step, this algorithm makes at most $$$\log_2 n$$$ recursive calls. In each recursive call, a binary search is done that takes at most $$$\log_2 n$$$ queries. Thus, the algorithm uses at most $$$(\log_2 n)^2 \lt 300$$$ queries in total.

Optionally, one can derive a tighter bound as follows. The sizes of the arrays are at most $$$n, n/2, n/4, \ldots$$$; then the total number of queries is at most $$$$$$ \log_2 n + \log_2 (n/2) + \log_2 (n/4) + \cdots + 1 = \log_2 n + (\log_2 (n) - 1) + (\log_2 (n) - 2) + \cdots + 1, $$$$$$ which is the sum of the integers from $$$1$$$ to $$$\log_2 n$$$ (assume, e.g., we are taking the ceilings of the logs), $$$$$$\frac{(\log_2 n)(\log_2 n - 1)}{2} \lt \frac{(\log_2 n)^2}{2} \lt 145.$$$$$$ Therefore, our recursive algorithm actually fits very comfortably within the query limit.
How would you write a validator for this problem? That is, given $$$n$$$ and an array $$$a$$$, determine if it can be generated by the described operations.
Try drawing the operation on some not small graphs!
What are the invariants of the operation?
The number of white vertices does not change. It also seems a lot of white vertices don't move or only move to a neighboring vertex.
In a single operation, what are some shared properties of the vertices whose color changed?
Color changes only occur within the detached subtree (why?) and it is a necessary condition that a vertex with a new color has a new parent.
Based on Hint 2, try to characterize the set of edges that cannot be removed no matter what operations are applied.
The parent edge of any black vertex cannot be removed (why?). Any other edge can be freely added and removed as long as T is a tree.
Consider the connected components formed by the parent edge of all black vertices (in other words, after cutting the parent edge of any white vertex). Which vertex is white within this component?
Exactly one vertex is white and it is the one closest to the root.
condition mean in terms of these connected components?
Read the hints for an intuitive walkthrough!

Consider the components formed after removing all edges connecting a white vertex and its parent. Note that naturally, every component has exactly one white vertex and it is the vertex closest to the root.
Claim: The above property is an invariant of the operation (that is, the components will always remain the same and a vertex is white iff it is the one closest to the root within a component).

Proof: In order to prove this, we will use the fact that every component has even size and every vertex has odd degree (with the exception of the component containing vertex $$$1$$$). You should try to prove why this is the case!

Suppose the operation was applied a single time, we will show that the invariant still holds. First, note that a single operation cannot break apart a component as the only removable edge is one connecting a white vertex and its parent (which is in a different component). After the operation, consider any component that is a leaf (that is, does not have any other component as a descendant).
If this is the component containing vertex $$$1$$$, note that this component could not have changed as a result of the operation and thus we are done.

Otherwise, the component has even size and thus the root of the subtree (that is, the vertex closest to the root) is colored white. It suffices to show that there are no other white vertices. Assume otherwise for the sake of contradiction that there exists another white vertex and consider the white vertex with greatest depth. The degree of this vertex is odd and thus it must have an even number of children. However, every child must be colored black since otherwise there would be a white vertex with greater depth. If a vertex has an even number of odd sized subtrees, its own subtree must also have odd size and we have a contradiction.

Now, in the latter case, because a subtree of even size does not affect the colors of any of its ancestors, we can remove the component and repeatedly apply the above reasoning. Thus, we've shown that the invariant holds. $$$\square$$$

So what kinds of trees can Yuuki construct? A corollary of the above claim is that any edge within a component cannot be removed. It turns out Yuuki can make any tree as long as no edges are removed within a component. Here is one possible method of constructing any tree: remove leaf components one by one and attach them to vertex $$$1$$$, then reassemble the now independent components as desired.

Let there be $$$k$$$ components $$$c_1\ldots c_k$$$ and their sizes be $$$s_1\ldots s_k$$$ (where $$$c_1$$$ contains vertex $$$1$$$). In order to satisfy the conquered condition, the components must be in a line with $$$c_1$$$ as an endpoint.
If $$$k=1$$$, then no operations can be applied and the answer is $$$1$$$.

Otherwise, $$$c_1$$$ must be one endpoint of the line and suppose $$$c_i$$$ ($$$2\le i\le k$$$) is the other endpoint. First, we get to reorder the internal components of the line in any way. For the two endpoint components, we must choose one vertex that is connected to its neighbor. For the internal components, we must choose two vertices, one for each neighbor. Therefore, the number of conquered trees is $$$$$$(k-2)!\cdot s_1\cdot s_i\cdot \prod_{j\not\in\{1, i\}}s_j^2$$$$$$ Taking the sum over all $$$i$$$, we get $$$$$$\sum_{i=2}^k\left((k-2)!\cdot s_1\cdot s_i\cdot \prod_{j\not\in\{1, i\}}s_j^2\right)=(k-2)!\cdot s_1\cdot \left(\sum_{i=2}^k\frac{1}{s_i}\right)\left(\prod_{i=2}^ks_i^2\right)$$$$$$
The sizes of the components can be found via DFS which, along with the above formula, can be computed in $$$O(n)$$$.
Try to solve the problem for only $$$\ell=n$$$.
Figure out how to count the number of chains containing a specific chord (without caring about complexity)

Any chain containing a specific chord can be decomposed into a chain ending at the chord and a chain starting at the chord. Because these parts are independent the number of chains is [number of chains ending at the chord] x [number of chains starting at the chord].
Figure out how we can compute the number of chains ending at chord $$$1\ldots n$$$ in quadratic time.

For a given chord $$$j$$$, the number of chains ending at $$$j$$$ is the sum of number of chains ending at chord $$$i \lt j$$$ for every chord $$$i$$$ that intersects chord $$$j$$$ plus one (for the chain consisting of just $$$j$$$)
You only care about parity. Figure out how to speed this up to $$$O(n\log n)$$$.

Consider an XOR Fenwick Tree of size $$$2n$$$, where at $$$x_i$$$ and $$$y_i$$$ you store the parity of number of chains ending at chord $$$I$$$. Then, the value in Hint 1.2 can be found by a range XOR query over $$$[x_j, y_j]$$$ because any chord not intersecting chord $$$j$$$ will either be accounted for $$$0$$$ or $$$2$$$ times.

The problem forces you to incrementally compute the values for $$$\ell=1\ldots n$$$. Try to solve the problem in quadratic or cubic time while only allowing yourself to consider the chords in order (i.e. you're not allowed to go backwards to compute the number of chains starting at a given chord).

In addition to storing the parity of number of chains ending at chord $$$i$$$, also store the set of chords $$$k \lt i$$$ such that chord $$$k$$$ appears in an odd number of chains ending at chord $$$i$$$. Then, for a fixed $$$\ell$$$, we want to check whether every chord appears in an even number of sets (this can all be done with $$$n$$$ Fenwick trees, one for each chord).
You have yet to use the fact that we want
chord to appear an even number of times (that is, we do not need to know the specific parity for each chord). Use this to speed the solution up to $$$O(n\log n)$$$.

The first key observation is that computation in $$$\mathbb{Z}_2$$$ works very nicely with chords. In particular, if you have bit string of length $$$2n$$$ and set the bits $$$x_i$$$ and $$$y_i$$$ to $$$1$$$ for some chord $$$i$$$, a range XOR query over the range $$$[x_j,y_j]$$$ for some chord $$$j$$$ will only count the contribution from chord $$$i$$$ if chord $$$i$$$ intersects chord $$$j$$$ (if they do not intersect, the indices $$$x_i$$$ and $$$y_i$$$ will appear either not appear or appear twice and cancel itself out). By this observation, using an XOR Fenwick Tree, we can compute $$$f(i)=(\text{number of }\textit{chains}\text{ ending at chord }i)\text{ mod } 2$$$ efficiently.

Now, consider the following solution that is too slow. For every $$$1\le i, j\le n$$$, let $$$$$$g(i,j)=(\text{number of }\textit{chains} \text{ containing chord }j\text{ and ending at chord }i)\text{ mod } 2$$$$$$ We can check whether the chords are tight-knit by checking whether $$$$$$\oplus_{i=j}^\ell g(i,j)=0\qquad\forall 1\leq j\leq \ell$$$$$$ We can compute the values of $$$g(i,j)$$$ as follows: $$$$$$ g(i,j)= \begin{cases} 0 & i \lt j\\ f(i) & i=j\\ \oplus_{k \lt i\text{ and chord }k\text{ intersects chord } i} g(k, j)& \text{otherwise} \end{cases} $$$$$$ Notably, computing for the last case can be optimized using the initial key observation. Using a Fenwick Tree of ✨ bitsets ✨, we can speed up the solution to $$$O(\frac{n^2}{w})$$$, but it will MLE/TLE.

In order to speed this up further, we will use the fact that we need every chord to appear an even number of times (and do not necessarily need to know the parities of each individual one). Define $$$$$$h(i)=\{j : f(i,j)=1\}$$$$$$ Now, we want to check whether $$$$$$\oplus_{i=1}^\ell h(i)=\emptyset$$$$$$ and we can compute $$$$$$ h(i)=\left(\oplus_{k \lt i\text{ and chord }k\text{ intersects chord } i} h(k)\right)\oplus \left(\{i\}\text{ if }f(i)=1\text{ else }\{\}\right) $$$$$$
However, it is obviously not possible to store and update these sets naively. What magical method can we use to store these sets efficiently? XOR Hashing!

If we compute a random $$$64$$$-bit hash for each chord, we can express a set as the XOR of the hashes of its elements. We can compute a symmetric difference of two sets by taking the XOR of its hashes. Thus, if we maintain two XOR Fenwick Trees (one for $$$f(i)$$$ and one for the hashes of $$$h(i)$$$), we can perform all updates in $$$O(\log n)$$$ and solve the problem in $$$O(n\log n)$$$.
The operation is clearly independent for each present. Solve the problem for a single type of present with value $$$a$$$.

Consider a graph with vertices $$$0\ldots m-1$$$. We draw an edge from $$$x \to (x+a) \text{ mod } m$$$ with cost $$$a$$$ and an edge from $$$x \to 2\cdot x \text{ mod } m$$$ with cost $$$k$$$. The desired answer is the shortest path from $$$a$$$ to $$$0$$$. However, it is not possible to combine the results for all three types without $$$O(n^2)$$$ $$$(\min, +)$$$ convolution.
There is one big idea that you need from here, the following small hints may help in getting you there.
It may be easier to start with no presents (but eventually force yourself to have all three).
Although we considered the operations for a given type of present independently from other types in Hint 1, we are allowed to intertwine operations as we wish.
If we tried to merge all three presents into a single graph, the primary issue is that we need to maintain three separate modulos to handle the duplicate spell. Is there any way we can fix this?
The operations are independent for each present so we'll consider them separately. First, we will solve the easier version of only one present type with value $$$a$$$.

When applying an operation, we only care about the current residue of the total sum modulo $$$m$$$. This motivates us to have some DP with this residue as the state. Let $$$dp[x]$$$ denote the minimum cost of a sequence of operations to get to $$$x\text{ mod }m$$$. We have $$$dp[a]=0$$$ and the transitions
$$$dp[x+a\text{ mod } m]=\min(dp[x + a\text{ mod } m], dp[x] + a)$$$ for the Create spell
$$$dp[x\cdot 2\text{ mod } m]=\min(dp[x \cdot 2\text{ mod } m], dp[x] + k)$$$ for the Duplicate spell

Because there is no nice way to iterate over $$$x$$$ in computing these transitions, we must consider a weighted graph representation (states as vertices and transitions as edges). In this graph representation, we can use Dijkstra's algorithm to find the shortest paths from vertex $$$0$$$ which give us the desired $$$dp$$$ values.
We could try to combine the results from above for $$$a$$$, $$$b$$$, and $$$c$$$. However, this would require a $$$(\min, +)$$$ convolution without a nice structure, which will take $$$O(n^2)$$$.

The issue that prevents us from making a graph representation that combines $$$a$$$, $$$b$$$, and $$$c$$$ is that we must maintain separate residues for each value in order to perform updates for the Duplicate spell. For instance, consider the following sequence of spells

If we only maintain a single combined residue, we do not know how to update our total value when duplicating a single present. To fix this, instead of considering the operations independently, we will perform them together. For instance, consider the following modification of the same sequence

This almost works, where we can duplicate presents together and simply double the combined residue. However, because we started with one of each present, we would be duplicating presents that we do not wish to. To fix this, we can just start with no presents and eventually force ourselves to create one of each present (and subtract $$$a+b+c$$$ from the cost at the end).
Thus, consider the graph with vertices $$$(\text{current residue}, \text{mask of presents we have at least one of})$$$. Then, we can create the following edges
The desired answer is the shortest path from $$$(0, 000)$$$ to $$$(0, 111)$$$, subtracted by $$$a+b+c$$$. This can be found using Dijkstra's algorithm in $$$O(8m\log m)$$$.
The input essentially just creates a graph, where cities are connected if they are at distanct $$$\sqrt{k}$$$. Can you find any special properties that this graph has?

Consider a graph on $$$n$$$ vertices corresponding to the cities in the input, where two cities have an edge between them if they have distance $$$\sqrt{k}$$$.

The first thing to note is that the graph is bipartite. To see this, note that if $$$k$$$ is odd and we color the board in a checkerboard pattern then all edges will be between a black and a white cell. The graph is thus bipartite. On the other hand, if $$$k$$$ is even, note that all edges will be between two white cells or between two black cells. We can consider these cases to be independent graphs. If we rotate either of these graphs by 45 degrees and scale down by a factor of $$$\sqrt{2}$$$, we again get a new lattice, except $$$k$$$ has halved. If we repeatedly do this until $$$k$$$ is odd, we can see that the original graph is a disjoint union of bipartite graphs and thus must be bipartite.

From here we can 2-color the graph into two parts $$$A$$$ and $$$B$$$. We can assign them such that $$$|A| \leq |B|$$$ (so $$$|A| \leq 15$$$). We iterate over subsets of $$$A'$$$ of $$$A$$$ that we place fireworks in. Note that the product of $$$1+[\text{number of adjacent fireworks}]$$$ can be reformulated as: the number of ways to select $$$0$$$ or $$$1$$$ adjacent fireworks for each city not in $$$T$$$. In other words, for each element not in $$$T$$$ we choose either nothing, or an adjacent city with fireworks.

Thus, we get the following dp approach: $$$\text{dp}[i][\text{mask}]$$$ is the sum of explosiveness after accounting for $$$b_1,\dots,b_i$$$ and mask represents which of the unplaced points in $$$A \setminus A'$$$ have selected an adjacent firework.

The transition from $$$i$$$ to $$$i+1$$$ is: $$$$$$\text{dp}[i+1][\text{mask}]~\text{+=}~\text{dp}[i][\text{mask}] \cdot [1+\text{number of fireworks in }A\text{ that are adjacent to }b_{i+1}]$$$$$$ for the cases where we don't place a firework at $$$b_{i+1}$$$. When we do place a firework, the transition is $$$$$$\text{dp}[i+1][\text{mask} | s]~\text{+=}~\text{dp}[i][\text{mask}]$$$$$$ where $$$s$$$ is a submask of the unplaced points adjacent to $$$b_{i+1}$$$ and $$$s\&mask=0$$$ (this corresponds to the points represented by $$$s$$$ selecting $$$b_{i+1}$$$ as their adjacent firework).

The final total that we want is the sum of $$$\text{dp}[|B|-1][\text{mask}]$$$ over all masks (and then we sum that value over all subsets $$$A'$$$ of $$$A$$$). For each $$$A'$$$, the time complexity is $$$\mathcal{O}(|B|*3^{|A'|})$$$. Summing over all $$$A'$$$, the overall complexity is $$$\mathcal{O}(|B|*4^{|A|})$$$, which needs to be optimized.

In order to speed this up note that the bottleneck is iterating over $$$s$$$ for the $$$\text{dp}[i+1][\text{mask}|s]~\text{+=}~\text{dp}[i][\text{mask}]$$$ transition. In particular, $$$\text{dp}[i+1][\text{mask1}]$$$ gets incremented by $$$\text{dp}[i+1][\text{mask2}]$$$ if and only if $$$\text{mask1}\wedge\text{mask2}$$$ is a submask of the unplaced points adjacent to $$$b_{i+1}$$$. This is exactly the result of a sum-over-subsets dp over the points adjacent to $$$b_{i+1}$$$. This means that the trasition for each $$$b_i$$$ will run in time $$$\mathcal{O}(\deg{b_i}2^{|A'|})$$$, so for each $$$A'$$$, the complexity will be $$$\mathcal{O}(\sum_{b_i \in B} \deg{b_i}\cdot 2^{|A'|}) = \mathcal{O}(|E(G)| \cdot 2^{|A'|})$$$. Summing over all $$$A'$$$ we get that the overall complexity is $$$\mathcal{O}(|E(G)| \cdot 3^{|A|})$$$ which we can upper bound by $$$|A||B|\cdot3^{|A|} = 240 \cdot 3^{15} \approx 3 \cdot 10^9$$$ which should pass with the given time limit (especially given that out innerloop contains only simple operations from the sum-over-subsets DP if we take care to mod only at the end).

To be more sure the above solution passes, we can show a better bound for $$$|E(G)|$$$. Note that the input graph cannot contain a $$$K_{2, 3}$$$ (as two circles in a plane intersect in at most two points). This means that $$$\sum \deg(b_i)^2 \leq 2 \binom{|A|}{2}$$$, so in the worst case $$$|A| = 15$$$ we get that $$$\sum \binom{\deg{b_i}}2 \leq 210 = 10 \cdot 15 + 6 \cdot 10$$$, so $$$\sum \deg(b_i) \leq 10 \cdot 6 + 6 \cdot 5 = 90$$$. (Note the inequality follows from seeing that if we look at pairs of adjacent vertices from each $$$b_i$$$, each pair of $$$a_i$$$ appears at most twice. The second inequality follows from convexity of $$$\binom{x}{2}$$$).

This gives us a bound of $$$|E(G)| \leq 90$$$. In the actual testdata, the worst case we found was $$$|E(G)| = 76$$$. Plugging in this value tells us that our same solution from before runs in under $$$10^9$$$ operations (which are mainly arithmetic and bitwise), which should easily pass.
